title: Baselines in linear vs iterative life cycles
blurb: State how the deployment baseline differs between linear and iterative life cycles: what is fixed, what flexes and when it is set.
question: A council is running two projects: a new footbridge using a linear life cycle and a parking-permit app using an iterative one. How will the deployment baseline differ between them, and which elements are fixed in each?

teach.body: Every project needs a baseline to measure delivery against, but linear and iterative life cycles set it differently. In a LINEAR life cycle the deployment baseline is set for the WHOLE project at the end of definition, with SCOPE FIXED and changes formally controlled. In an ITERATIVE life cycle TIME and COST are FIXED and SCOPE FLEXES, while quality is protected: a high-level baseline is set first, then detailed baselines time box by time box.

rows.label: Covers
values: High level, then each time box

rows.label: Flexes
values: Time and cost, via change control

teach.h: What is fixed and what flexes
teach.caption: Linear: fix what is delivered, and time and cost follow from it. Iterative: fix the time and money, and deliver the highest-priority scope that fits.

teach.h: Linear: one baseline for the whole project
teach.body: In a linear project, requirements are defined in detail during definition. The WBS, schedule, budget and resources are planned for all the work, and the sponsor approves a single deployment baseline covering the whole project. Scope is fixed. Any later request to change it goes through formal change control, and an approved change may move the time and cost baseline.

teach.h: Iterative: fixed time and cost, flexible scope
teach.body: In an iterative project, foundations set a HIGH-LEVEL baseline: the overall timescale, budget and plan of time boxes, plus prioritised requirements (MoSCoW). The DETAILED baseline is then set time box by time box, as the team agrees which requirements it will deliver next. If time runs short, lower-priority scope is dropped or deferred: the end date and cost do not move.

teach.h: Iterative: baselined time box by time box
teach.caption: Every time box has fixed dates and cost. What it delivers is agreed at its start, from the highest-priority requirements.

teach.h: Worked scenario: the same request in two projects
head: Aspect
Footbridge (linear)
Permit app (iterative)
rows: Goes into a later time box

teach.text: In an iterative baseline, TIME and COST are fixed. An option saying 'scope and quality are fixed' in an iterative baseline is wrong because SCOPE is what flexes. Quality is protected, never traded away: the features delivered change, not the standard they meet. And 'flexible' does not mean 'no baseline': iterative projects still baseline, just at a high level and then per time box.

items: Linear: one deployment baseline for the whole project, set at the end of definition, scope fixed.
Linear changes go through formal change control; time and cost may then move.
Iterative: time and cost fixed, scope flexes; high-level baseline, then detailed baselines per time box.
Iterative changes are absorbed by reprioritising requirements (MoSCoW) between time boxes.

summary: You can now state that a linear life cycle sets one deployment baseline for the whole project with scope fixed, while an iterative life cycle fixes time and cost, lets scope flex and baselines in detail time box by time box. You can explain how change is handled in each.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, what does the deployment baseline cover?
options: One time box at a time, with scope flexing
Only the concept phase of the work
The whole project, with scope fixed
The benefits after the project closes
A.why: A linear project sets one deployment baseline for the whole project, at the end of definition, with scope fixed.

whyNot.0: Baselining one time box at a time with flexing scope describes an iterative life cycle.
whyNot.1: Concept comes before the baseline is set; the baseline covers deployment of the whole project.
whyNot.3: Benefits after closure are tracked by benefits management, not the deployment baseline.

A.q: In an iterative life cycle, which elements are normally fixed in the baseline?
A.why: Iterative projects fix time and cost; scope flexes to fit them.

whyNot.0: Scope is the element that flexes in an iterative project, so this cannot be right. Quality is protected, but it is time and cost that are fixed in the baseline.
whyNot.2: Cost is fixed, but scope is not.
whyNot.3: Time is fixed, but scope is not.

A.q: Complete the statement: in an iterative project, detailed deployment baselines are set ____.
options: once, at the end of definition
A.why: After a high-level baseline at foundations, detailed baselines are set for each time box as requirements are prioritised.

whyNot.0: One baseline set at the end of definition describes a linear life cycle.
whyNot.1: Transition is a linear phase name, and a baseline after it would be pointless.
whyNot.2: The PMO does not set baselines, and closure is far too late.

B.q: Which statement describes a key difference between linear and iterative deployment baselines?
options: Only iterative projects have a baseline
Linear fixes scope; iterative fixes time and cost
Iterative fixes scope; linear fixes time and cost
Only linear projects need any form of control
B.why: Linear projects fix scope for the whole project; iterative projects fix time and cost and let scope flex.

whyNot.0: Both life cycles use a baseline; they set it differently.
whyNot.2: This is the wrong way round.
whyNot.3: Both need control; iterative projects control change by reprioritising scope within fixed time and cost.

B.q: In an iterative project, a time box is running short of time. What normally happens?
options: The time box end date is extended
Extra budget is added to finish it
B.why: Time and cost are fixed, so lower-priority requirements are dropped or deferred to protect the date.

whyNot.0: Extending the date breaks the fixed time that defines a time box.
whyNot.1: Cost is fixed in an iterative baseline, so adding budget is not the normal response.
whyNot.3: Running short in one time box does not cancel the baseline; scope is simply reprioritised.

B.q: Why is a single whole-project baseline well suited to a linear life cycle?
options: Requirements are stable and defined early
Users want to change features each week
The budget is unknown until handover
There is no need to monitor progress
B.why: Linear projects suit stable, well-understood requirements, so the whole scope can be defined and fixed at the end of definition.

whyNot.1: Frequently changing features suit an iterative approach, not a single fixed baseline.
whyNot.2: A linear baseline includes an approved budget before deployment starts.
whyNot.3: The whole point of a baseline is to monitor progress against it.

C.q:
A council runs a footbridge project (linear) and a booking app project (iterative). Which TWO statements are correct?
1) The footbridge baseline covers the whole project, set at the end of definition
2) The app's scope is fixed and its end date flexes
3) The app's detailed baseline is set for each time box
4) Footbridge scope changes are absorbed by reprioritising a backlog
C.why: The linear footbridge has one whole-project baseline (1), and the iterative app is baselined in detail time box by time box (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: in the iterative app, time is fixed and scope flexes.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: 2 reverses the iterative rule, and 4 describes iterative, not linear, change.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: linear scope changes go through formal change control.

C.q: Midway through an iterative project, the product owner swaps a new 'must have' feature in place of a 'could have'. What happens to the time and cost baseline?
C.why: In an iterative project, time and cost are fixed; the swap is absorbed by changing scope, not by moving time or cost.

whyNot.1: Increasing time and cost would break the fixed elements of an iterative baseline.
whyNot.2: Cost is fixed as well as time.
whyNot.3: Time is fixed as well as cost.

C.q: On a linear project, the client asks for extra scope during deployment. How is the baseline protected?
options: The team simply absorbs the extra work
The scope is reprioritised using MoSCoW
The next time box is shortened to fit it
The request goes through change control
C.why: In a linear project scope is fixed in the baseline, so any change is captured, evaluated and decided through formal change control.

whyNot.0: Absorbing unapproved work causes scope creep and hides variance from the baseline.
whyNot.1: Reprioritising with MoSCoW is how iterative projects absorb change.
whyNot.2: Time boxes belong to iterative life cycles, not a linear one.

reteach.title: A banquet menu vs a weekly food shop
reteach.question: Compare ordering a fixed banquet menu months ahead with doing a food shop each week on a fixed budget. Which is like a linear baseline, and which is like an iterative one?

blocks.h: Fix the menu, or fix the budget?
blocks.body: For a banquet, you agree the whole menu with the caterer months ahead. The menu is fixed, and if you add a course you formally amend the contract and pay more. That is LINEAR. For a weekly shop, you have £100 and must shop by Saturday. Money and time are fixed; what goes in the basket changes each week, must-haves first. That is ITERATIVE.

blocks.text: The weekly shop still has a plan: a budget, a deadline and a priority list. Iterative does not mean unplanned; it means the detail is planned one time box at a time.

explain.body: Set once, at the end of definition, for the whole project. Scope is fixed; time and cost are derived from it and may move only through approved change control.

test.q: When is a linear project's deployment baseline normally set?
options: At the start of each sprint
test.why: In a linear life cycle the whole-project baseline is approved at the end of definition, before deployment begins.

whyNot.1: Setting a baseline per sprint or time box is the iterative approach.
whyNot.2: Transition is handover; the baseline is needed long before.
whyNot.3: Benefits review happens after delivery and does not set the baseline.

explain.body: In an iterative baseline, time and cost (with the team's resources) are fixed. Scope, meaning which features are delivered, is the element that flexes. Quality is protected: agreed acceptance standards are not traded away to fit the time box.

test.q: Which element flexes in an iterative deployment baseline?
test.why: Scope flexes in an iterative baseline, while time, cost and the team's resources stay fixed.

whyNot.0: Time is fixed in an iterative baseline.
whyNot.1: Cost is fixed in an iterative baseline.
whyNot.3: Resources are held fixed for each time box; scope is what flexes.

explain.body: Foundations set a high-level baseline: overall time, budget, time box plan and prioritised requirements. Each time box then gets its own detailed baseline when the team commits to what it will deliver.

levels.label: Detailed baselines
levels.sub: set time box by time box

test.q: What is set at foundations in an iterative project, before the time boxes begin?
options: A detailed baseline for every feature
A high-level baseline of time and cost
The final scope, which cannot change
The report from the benefits review
test.why: Foundations establish the high-level baseline: overall time, cost, the time box plan and prioritised requirements.

whyNot.0: Detail is baselined later, one time box at a time.
whyNot.2: Scope is not frozen in an iterative project; it flexes.
whyNot.3: A benefits review comes after delivery, not at foundations.

explain.body: Linear: change requests go through formal change control and, if approved, the whole-project baseline is updated. Iterative: new requirements are added to the backlog and prioritised for a later time box, with time and cost unchanged.

test.q: On an iterative project, how is a new requirement normally absorbed?
test.why: Iterative projects absorb change by reprioritising requirements, so time and cost stay fixed.

whyNot.0: Time is fixed, so extending the deadline is not the normal route.
whyNot.1: Cost is fixed, so raising the budget is not the normal route.
whyNot.2: A single new requirement does not mean revisiting the whole business case.
